subtype: Approach: seeking a mentor and campus incubator advice [Action]
passage: Thursday, 10 pm. Today was our incubator slot. Steps: (1) Omkar and I cut our pitch to five slides. (2) We showed the mentor how the laundry service runs and what we charge. (3) The mentor asked how many paying customers we have. Eleven. They nodded and said that was a start, but before we talk to investors we need many more paying pilots. (4) They explained in plain words what registering a business involves and roughly what the costs are, and suggested we check details with a professional when the time comes. I wrote it all down. Not scary. My action list for tomorrow: find 20 more pilot customers. — Lalit

qa.q: How many paying customers did Lalit and Omkar have?
What does Lalit feel about the mentor's advice?
qa.a: Lalit feels reassured and motivated, since the advice is not scary and comes with a clear action list.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the founders use alongside the mentor, and why?
qa.a: They could talk to a founder who has just started a similar service, because a mentor gives structure while a peer shows the daily reality.

qa.q: How might the mentor see the founders after this session?
qa.a: The mentor sees two founders with a real service and eleven paying customers who asked good questions, so the mentor points them to more paying pilots before any investors.

grounding: Shows seeking a mentor at a campus incubator, learning registration and cost basics, and hearing that paid pilots must come before investors.
